cards.text: Every tribe in Israel has its land now, except the Levites, whose share is the priesthood of the LORD instead of a chunk of land (Joshua 18:7; 19:51). So at Shiloh, the Levite family heads walk up to Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, Israel's leader, and the heads of the other tribes. They bring up a command the LORD gave.

cards.question: The Levite leaders say the LORD gave a command about them. Who did the LORD give that command through?
The Levites have no land of their own. What does the LORD's command say they should be given?

answers.text: A share of the war spoils

cards.question: Along with the cities, the Levites ask for pasturelands for their ___.
So how do the tribes of Israel answer the Levites' request for cities?

answers.text: They give cities out of their own land
They tell the Levites to wait a year
They point them to land not yet conquered

cards.question: The Israelites give the Levites these cities by the command of the LORD.

cards.text: That's a LOT of city names, friend, so I'll spare you the roll call. The cities are handed out by lot, clan by clan, from all the other tribes: first Aaron's descendants, the priests, then the rest of Kohath's clans, then Gershon's, then Merari's. The priests get Hebron, though its fields and villages had already gone to Caleb son of Jephunneh, and cities of refuge like Hebron and Shechem are on the list too. Forty-eight cities in all, and every one of them has its own pasturelands (Joshua 21:41-42).

Now the writer steps back from all those city names to look at the whole picture, like me stepping back to admire a counter full of sealed cookie boxes. And it starts with the land the LORD swore to give Israel's fathers.

cards.question: How much of the land He swore to Israel's fathers does the LORD give Israel?
Once the LORD gives Israel the land, they take possession of it and settle in it.
Just as He swore to their fathers, the LORD gives Israel ___ on every side.
None of Israel's enemies can stand against them. Why not?

answers.text: The LORD handed them all over to Israel
Israel's army had grown too big to beat
Every enemy signed a peace treaty

cards.text: The chapter ends with one more line, about all the good promises the LORD made to the house of Israel.

cards.question: A few of the LORD's good promises to the house of Israel had failed.

cards.text: Not ONE failed. Everything was fulfilled. Friend, I once promised a baker a batch by noon and pulled it out at a quarter after, and I'm STILL hearing about it. The LORD's record? Perfect.

findings.problem: The wrong answers 'gardens' and 'visitors' aren't the same kind of thing as 'livestock' and don't fit pasturelands. 'Pasturelands for their visitors' reads as silly, so 'livestock' stands out and the card tests nothing.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: Caleb, Kohath, Gershon and Merari appear here for the first time, and the card never says simply who they are. 'Caleb son of Jephunneh' gives only his father's name. Kohath, Gershon and Merari get no description at all, such as Levi's sons whose families became the Levite clans.

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'Every enemy signed a peace treaty' sounds modern next to the other two answers, which makes it easy to rule out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences. It isn't the opening card or a summary card for a long stretch, so it can have only 1 to 2.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Only card 15 has a real laugh. Cards 1 and 13 are plain narration. Card 8's cookie-box comparison reads like a nice dad being pleasant. The opening moment, where the Levites walk up and remind everyone of a command, could hold a joke without muddying a fact.

rule.text: When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
